Emerging low-dimensional perovskite resistive
switching memristors: from fundamentals to
devices
Shuanglong Wang1, Hong Lian2, Haifeng Ling3, Hao Wu4,
Tianxiao Xiao1,5,6*, Yijia Huang7* and Peter Müller-Buschbaum5*
With the exponential growth of the internet of things, artificial intelligence, and energy-efficient high-volume data digital
communications, there is an urgent demand to develop new information technologies with high storage capacity. This
needs to address the looming challenge of conventional Von Neumann architecture and Moore's law bottleneck for fu-
ture data-intensive computing applications. A promising remedy lies in memristors, which offer distinct advantages of
scalability, rapid access times, stable data retention, low power consumption, multistate storage capability and fast oper-
ation. Among the various materials used for active layers in memristors, low dimensional perovskite semiconductors with
structural diversity and superior stability exhibit great potential for next generation memristor applications, leveraging hys-
teresis characteristics caused by ion migration and defects. In this review the progress of low-dimensional perovskite
memory devices is comprehensively summarized. The working mechanism and fundamental processes, including ion mi-
gration dynamics, charge carrier transport and electronic resistance that underlies the switching behavior of memristors
are discussed. Additionally, the device parameters are analyzed with special focus on the effective methods to improve
electrical performance and operational stability. Finally, the challenges and perspective on major hurdles of low-dimen-
sional perovskite memristors in the expansive application domains are provided.
Keywords: low dimensional perovskite; memristor; electrical parameters; Ion migration; operational stability

An obvious answer to circumvent this substantial lim-

processes.

Low-dimensional perovskites
Reducing  the  number  of  inorganic  layers  in  3D  per-
ovskite from infinity to certain values results in the low-
dimensional structure, as demonstrated in Fig. 2(a). The
adjacent  inorganic  sheets  aligned  with  face-sharing  ar-
chitecture  are  called  one-dimensional  (1D)  perovskite.
2D  or  quasi-2D  organic-inorganic  hybrid  perovskites
can  be  obtained  by  intercalating  organic  ligands  along
the  (100)  plane  of  the  parent  3D  cubic  perovskites42.
These  structures  exhibit  a  typical  self-assembly  multi-
quantum  well  configuration  with  alternating  bulky  or-
ganic spacer cations and corner-sharing inorganic sheets
[BX6]4−, which the inorganic layer can be considered as a
quantum well and the spacer cation layer acts as a quan-
tum barrier43. Figure 2(b) shows the chemical structures
of classic bulky organic cations used in 2D perovskites.
Notably,  these  low-dimensional  perovskites  maintain
many  of  the  key  fascinating  features  of  3D  perovskites
and  can  be  synthesized  by  modulating  the  molar  ratio
between A-site small size cations and bulky spacers. Note
that  some  recent  reported  2D  perovskites  are  all-inor-
ganic  structures  by  using  inorganic  spacer  cations.  To-
day, organic-inorganic hybrid 2D structures are heavily
investigated in optoelectronic devices44. This trend is as-
cribed to the chemical nature of organic cations, which
opens-up  a  plethora  of  opportunities  for  synthetic
chemists to explore various chemical structures.
Interestingly,  due  to  the  high  dielectric  contrast  be-
tween  the  organic  ligands  and  inorganic  sheets,  charge
carrier  transport  is  confined  in  the  inorganic  [BX6]4−
part45,46.  Therefore,  by  controlling  the  thickness  of  the

Ion migration in perovskite
semiconductors
The RS phenomenon in memristors is closely related to
the ion migration behavior of perovskite materials49. Ion
migration effect in perovskite semiconductors has been
regarded  as  one  of  the  most  interesting  processes.  Per-
ovskite materials are generally considered as mixed con-
ductors with hybrid ionic and electronic characteristics.
The ionic movement cannot be neglected in perovskite
devices due to a large fraction of mobile ions in these soft
ionic materials. Previous studies have indicated that such
"mobile  ion"  has  been  implicated  as  the  cause  of  many
important  properties  associated  with  perovskites  in  the
devices, such as current-voltage hysteresis, structural in-
stability,  phase  separation,  thermoelectricity,  ferroelec-
tricity, etc50−54. For example, ion migration and accumu-
lation contribute to the anomalous phenomena such as
hysteresis, and giant capacitance in solar cells, and also
hold  the  responsible  for  poor  operation  stability  of  the
light-emitting devices55. However, ion migration is more
believed as a double-edged sword, as it also offers some
advantages  for  device  applications.  For  instance,  it  was
reported that the ion migration process was beneficial for
promoting the performance of solar cells under continu-
ous light illumination since the accumulation of mobile
ions can passivate traps at the interface, leading to im-
proved carrier transport and collection efficiency56. Ad-
ditionally,  fast-response  photodetectors  are  also  poten-
tial applications for perovskite materials due to the ma-
nipulation  of  ion  migration  progress  under  different
electric fields57. It should be pointed out that the ion mi-
gration  behavior  in  perovskites  is  highly  favorable  and
necessary for memristor applications, since it is involved
in the resistive switching (RS) property with the forma-
tion and rupture of conductive filaments or regulation of
interfacial energetic barriers, which will be discussed in
detail in Section Resistive switching mechanisms.
Theoretically, any of the constituting cations and an-
ions  in  perovskite  materials  can  migrate  under  certain
conditions (Fig. 3(a))58. For example, Haruyama et al. re-
ported  that  in  3D  perovskite  MAPbI3 films,  iodine  va-
cancies exhibit low activation energy of 0.3 eV based on
density functional theory calculations, as shown in Fig.
3(b)59.  The  calculated  activation  barrier  of  MA+ vacan-
cies, depicted in Fig. 3(c), is approximately 0.57 eV, The
above result suggests that both I− and MA+ can diffuse
intensely  under  external  stimuli.  Additional  extrinsic
ions resulting from decomposition or contamination of
perovskites  and  electrode  materials  by  electrochemical
reaction  with  semiconducting  layer,  such  as  H+,  or
metallic ions may also join the game. It is generally be-
lieved that ion migration dynamics are mediated by traps
and defects in perovskite films, similar to diffusion pro-
cesses60. Earlier studies revealed that the trap density Nt
in  single  crystalline  3D  organic-inorganic  hybrid  per-
ovskites is around 109−1010 cm−3 61. A higher density of
point  defects  can  be  generated  in  polycrystalline  per-
ovskite films by several origins, such as the rapid crystal-
lization of perovskite films prepared by solution process-
ing and the non-stoichiometry ratio between the precur-
sor  materials  in  solutions62.  The  point  defects  in  per-
ovskite  include  Schottky  and  Frenkel  defects  (Fig. 3(d)
and 3(e))63. These point defects can move from sites to
sites under an electric field. The first experimentally con-
firmed  migrating  species  as  point  defects  was  MA+ in
MAPbI3 perovskite  solar  cells  by  Yuan  et  al.  in  201564.

The operating principles of RS memory
devices
 
Device structure
Typical  memristor  devices  usually  exhibit  two-terminal
(2T)  diodes  or  three-terminal  transistor  geometries,  as
shown in Fig. 4(a). To date, the 2T structure is the main-
stream device structure, which is widely used and report-
ed in memristors. In this architecture, the perovskite ac-
tive  layer  is  sandwiched  between  the  bottom  and  top
electrodes on the substrate. Conventional metals, such as
Au, Ag, or indium tin oxide (ITO) are generally used in
bottom electrode materials67. In addition, active and in-
ert metals including Ag, Al, Pt and others are favorable
for top electrode applications. It is noteworthy that the
2T diode structure can be further divided into sandwich
and cross-array architectures. Currently, 2T cross-array
based memristors are widely reported since they can be
easily integrated into computing or synapse systems.
Based on the observed switching behavior in the I-V
characteristics,  memristors  can  be  classified  into  two
types: digital and analog68. Digital type memristors typi-
cally exhibit a current jump behavior in their I-V curves,
characterized  by  a  reversible  resistance  switching  and
stable performance, making them primarily suitable for
memory devices, as illustrated in Fig. 4(b). To date, most
reported perovskite memristors show a digital switching
behavior. In contrast, analog memristors demonstrate a
gradual current variation with continuous adjustable re-
sistance values, mimicking the functionality of synaptic
weights  (Fig. 4(c))69.  Consequently,  analog  memristors
are  commonly  used  to  simulate  synaptic  plasticity  and
enable neuromorphic computing, as they can modulate
their  resistance  over  a  continuous  range  of  voltage  or
current.  However,  analog  memristors  generally  exhibit
low stability and repeatability in their resistance switch-
ing, which remains a critical challenge for further opti-
mization and application70.
 
Resistive switching mode
Memristor devices generally exhibit a pinched hysteresis
loop in the current-voltage characteristic under the peri-
odic external stimulus of voltage or current. Based on the
different resistance states, such as a high resistance state
(HRS) or a low resistance state (LRS), the RS modes can
be classified as unipolar (nonpolar) and bipolar. For ex-
ample, a sharp increase in current is observed when the
swept positive voltage increases in Fig. 4(d), indicative of
the resistance transition from the HRS to the LRS. Simi-
larly, when a negative bias is applied, a sudden increase
occurs again in the resistance, returning the device back
to HRS71. Conversely, the bipolar RS mode has been ex-
tensively  studied  since  the  resistance  transition  can  be
activated  and  deactivated  by  applying  forward  and  re-
verse  bias,  respectively. Figure 4(e) illustrates  the  hys-
teresis  loop  of  current-voltage  curves  in  bipolar  mode-
based devices, where the switch between HRS and LRS
depends on the polarity of the applied voltage. The de-
velopment  of  bi- and  unipolar  memristors  is  crucial  to
meet  the  diverse  needs  of  these  applications.  Bipolar
memristors are particularly preferable for neuromorphic
computing and learning-based applications, as they en-
able  more  complex  behaviors  such  as  synaptic
plasticity73. In contrast, unipolar memristors are simpler
and  more  energy-efficient,  making  them  ideal  candi-
dates for basic memory and logic operations. The ongo-
ing  advancements  in  perovskite  memristor  technology
are likely to drive further innovation in these fields, con-
tributing to their commercialization and integration in-
to next-generation electronic systems. Figure 4(f) shows

Electrical parameters
There  are  several  key  electrical  parameters  that  deter-
mine  the  performance  of  a  memristor,  such  as  the
switching  current  ratio  (ION/IOFF),  threshold  voltage
(VTH), retention time, cycling endurance and multi‐re-
sistance states. These electrical parameters in memristor
devices can be significantly influenced by several factors
including  materials  property,  interlayer  and  electrode
materials74.  In  general,  a  large ION/IOFF,  low VTH,  high
retention time and long cycling endurance are prerequi-
sites  for  a  superior  memristor.  Switching  current  ratio
ION/IOFF refers to the ratio of current in the HRS to the
LRS.  A  large ION/IOFF value  indicates  the  high  reading
and  writing  accuracy  of  information75.  Threshold  volt-
age VTH refers to the switching voltage of the memristor,
including  the  write  voltage  (VSET)  that  transforms  the
HRS  to  the  LRS  and  the  rewrite  voltage  (VRESET)  with
LRS to HRS of the device, respectively. A low VSET and
VRESET suggest the low operating voltage in the device,
reduce power consumption in the system. Operating at a
low voltage reduces electrical and electrochemical stress
on  the  channel  material,  minimizing  physical  degrada-
tion  and  extending  the  device  lifespan76.  The  ability  of
memristor devices to retain data is mainly manifested by
retention  time.  High  retention  time  refers  to  the  long-
term  memory  capacity  of  the  device.  Long  cycling  en-
durance  means  that  the  memristor  can  change  steadily
between the reversible cycles of HRS and LRS, ensuring
the security of stored data. Both retention time and cy-
cling endurance are key parameters to evaluate the oper-
ational stability of memory devices. Additionally, except
for the LRS and HRS, an ideal memristor should also ex-
hibit  other  medium  resistance  states.  The  multi ‐resis-
tance states could ensure the accuracy and robustness of
memristors for neuromorphic operations77.
 
Resistive switching mechanisms
So far, extensive research on memristor devices has been
conducted to understand the RS mechanisms, which can
be classified into the electrochemical metallization mech-
anism  (ECM),  valence  change  mechanism  (VCM),  and
the interfacial charge transport. Both ECM and VCM be-
long  filamentary-type  mechanisms78. Figure 5(a) shows
the illustration of ECM of the memristors. ECM is de-
fined as the generation of metallic cation based conduct-
ing filaments by active metal electrode materials. During
resistive  switching  operation,  the  active  metal  first  oxi-
dizes into metallic cations under electric field and then
migrates  into  the  perovskite  layer.  A  conductive  metal
filament channel between the top and bottom electrodes
could be formed once these mobile ions reach the nega-
tive electrode, following the switching from HRS to LRS
in  memristor79.  On  the  other  hand,  the  melting  and
breaking processes of metal filament occur due to Joule
heating when a reverse bias is applied to the metal elec-
trode, leading to the device switching from LRS to HRS.
VCM refers to the phenomenon that negatively charged
ions such as I- and Br- migrate along the defect vacancies
under external bias in active layer (Fig. 5(b)). Halide an-
ions are generally believed to be the dominant ionic de-
fects  in  lead-based  3D  and  low-dimensional  perovskite
due  to  their  low  formation  energy80.  These  anions  in-
duced  conductive  channel  between  the  two  electrodes
can be formed or broken with a forward or reverse volt-
age, accompanied by the transition from the HRS to the
LRS or LRS to HRS in the device.
The interfacial charge transport mechanism is a non-
filamentary-type mechanism, where the resistive switch-
ing occurs at the interface between the electrode and ac-
tive layer or modification layer due to their energy level
barrier, as shown in Fig. 5(c). Zhou et al. reported a per-
ovskite  memristor  with  Au  top  electrode81.  Due  to  the
presence of hole traps between the perovskite and Au in-
terface,  hole  carriers  injected  and  filled  into  the  hole
trapping sites as the electric field increases. These accu-
mulated  holes  shifted  the  Fermi  level  of  the  perovskite
toward the valence band, reducing the Schottky barrier
and causing the device to switch from HRS to LRS. Addi-
tionally, the external bias required for SET operation of
the  perovskite  memristor  can  be  significantly  reduced
under illumination since the Schottky barrier at the in-
terface can be modified by trapping the photogenerated
carriers. This demonstrates the important role of Schot-
tky  junction  in  the  resistance  switching  mechanism
(Fig. 5(d)).

RP-type organic-inorganic hybrid 2D lead-free
perovskite
The toxicity issue of soluble lead salts in perovskite when
exposed  to  humans  raises  a  major  concern  about  their
commercialization success in electronics. Therefore, it is
highly desirable to find alternatives to replace lead com-
pounds in the long run. Previous work has shown that
the  less  toxic  ions,  including  Sn2+,  Bi3+,  Ge2+,  Sb3+,  and
Cu2+, which have similar atomic electronic configuration
to Pb2+, are promising candidates to realize lead-free per-
ovskite structures91−95. Kim et al. reported the first 2D or-
ganic-inorganic  hybrid  lead-free  perovskite  memristor,
demonstrating the bipolar resistive switching behavior of
(BzA)2CuBr4 (BzA = C6H5CH2NH3) perovskite96. Figure
8(a) shows  the  corresponding  device  structure  of
Ag/PMMA/(BzA)2CuBr4/Pt. From the I-V curve in Fig.
8(b), the VSET of 0.2 V, VRESET of −0.3 V and ION/OFF of
108 were  extracted,  respectively.  Interestingly,  the  ON
and OFF switching occurred at VSET of about 0.2 V and
at VRESET of  about −0.3  V  after  the  forming  step,  as
shown in Fig. 8(c) and 8(d). This phenomenon suggests
that RS behavior in (BzA)2CuBr4 memristor can be at-
tributed  to  a  filamentary-type  conduction  belonging  to
ECM. Owing to the oxidation of active Ag electrode, an
electroforming process is needed to stabilize the resistive
switching  properties.  Switching  endurance  was  mea-
sured  up  to  2000  cycles  where  the  retention  time  over
1000 s is retained, suggesting the great potential of Cu-
based perovskites in memristors (Fig. 8(e) and 8(f)).
Bismuth(III)-based  semiconductors  are  also  an  ap-
pealing class of materials among low-toxic or toxic-free
perovskites.  The  green  elemental  nature  of  Bi,  with  its
similar  ns2 electronic  configuration,  electronegativity,
and comparable ionic radius to Pb element, makes it a
promising alternative. It was reported that Bi-based dou-
ble  perovskites  with  the  crystal  structure  of  A2B+B3+X6,
such as benchmark Cs2AgBiBr6, exhibit outstanding sta-
bility and long carrier recombination lifetime97,98. Man-
dal's  group  reported  the  application  of  2D  lead-free
(BA)4AgBiBr8 perovskite in memristor devices99. The I-V
characteristics of the Au/(BA)4AgBiBr8/ITO in Fig. 8(g)
showed clear bipolar RS property with the VSET of 0.6 V,
VRESET of −0.5 V, ION/OFF of 106 and high reproducibili-
ty.  The  origin  of  memory  behavior  of  (BA)4AgBiBr8
based device was attributed to the charge trapping and
de-trapping occurred at the grain boundaries in the film,
as indicated by various characterizations. The data reten-

500  cycles  were  achieved,  as  presented  in Fig. 8(h).
Meanwhile, the device showed superior operational sta-
bility,  suggesting  the  reliable  memory  characteristics  of
2D (BA)4AgBiBr8 perovskite memristor (Fig. 8(i)).

inorganic elements, are expected to be more robust un-

mismatch is significantly reduced between the inorganic
frameworks and organic barriers as a consequence of the

different 2D structures (Fig. 9(b))102.

tures with diammonium organic ligands create a direct
connection between adjacent inorganic perovskite layers
by  hydrogen  bonding,  eliminating  the  van  der  Waals
gaps, This results in improved stability, which is essen-
tial  for  memristor  applications107.  Strikingly,  however,
only a few cases have been reported in the successful fab-
rication  of  2D  layered  DJ-type  perovskites  by  classic
spin-coating processing technique and their applications
in memory devices so far, which is ascribed to the lack of
DJ-type  cations  with  balanced  flexibility  and  rigidity,
leading to the poor phase purity and high density of de-
fects in the film108.
Park  et  al.  prepared  high-crystalline  2D  DJ  phase
(3AMP)PbI4 perovskite  thin  films  by  using  the  solvent
dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO)109. The electrical characteris-

the device was operated up to 1000 cycles without degra-

Conclusion
This section presents a summary of the effects of dimen-
sionality strategies on the electrical parameters of mem-
ristors, with a focus on modification of the material di-
mensions  from  1D  to  mixed  2D/3D  perovskites.  Based
on  the  above  results,  we  find  that  the  memristors  with
2D  and  quasi-2D  perovskite  show  superior  perfor-
mances.  Specifically,  the  edge  sharing  and  face-sharing
octahedral connectivity of the 1D perovskite phase pro-
vide limited charge-transport channels. In contrast, ex-
cept  for  the  environmental  stability  due  to  the  protec-
tion of large organic spacer cations, the 2D and quasi-2D
perovskite  memristors  exhibit  improved  endurance
properties and increased ION/OFF owing to much higher
Schottky  barriers  between  the  metal  electrode  and  the
perovskite  semiconducting  layer.  More  importantly,
compared  with  other  dimensional  perovskites,  the
anisotropic nature of 2D and quasi-2D functional layers
can significantly reduce the formation energy barrier of
conductive filaments along the defect channels. It is also
worth noting that the mixed 2D and 3D perovskites gen-
erally  contain  inconstant n values.  This  behavior  may
cause low homogeneity in the RS characteristics. There-
fore, future research attention should be paid to optimiz-
ing the trade-offs between enhanced stability and RS per-
formances in low-dimensional perovskite systems to fur-
ther advance their application in high-performance resis-
tive memory devices.
 
Summary and outlook
In recent years, perovskite memristors have gained sig-
nificant attention for their potential applications in low-
power  memory,  neuromorphic  computing,  and  various
Internet of Things applications. As the demand for ener-
gy-efficient and high-performance devices rises, the mar-
ket for perovskite memristors is expected to grow in the
future. In this review, we have predominantly focused on
the  state-of-the-art  progress  of  low-dimensional  per-
ovskites  memristor  and  highlighted  their  fundamental
properties,  including  electrical  parameters  and  stability
issues. In recent years, the importance of low-dimension-
al perovskites for memristor devices has become increas-
ingly prominent. Compared with conventional 3D per-
ovskites, the advantages of low-dimensional perovskites
primarily lie in their greatly enhanced operational stabil-
ity against water and oxygen due to the introduction of
bulky  organic  hydrophobic  ammonium  cations.  In  re-
viewing the literature, we have summarized that the di-
mensionalities, compositions, grain sizes, and interfacial
layers significantly alter the electronic properties of low-
dimensional perovskites, which are important for memo-
ry  applications.  Despite  progress  in  ON/OFF  ratio  and
environmental stability characteristics across low-dimen-
sional  perovskite  memristors,  there  is  still  considerable
scope for improving the endurance and retention time of
these devices. We believe the key areas for continued de-
velopment are as follows.
 
Rational design of novel organic ligands
The chemical nature of organic ligands significantly in-
fluences  the  electronic  properties  of  low-dimensional
perovskites  and  devices.  From  reviewing  the  literature,
we have identified the differences among reported spac-
er cations is mainly reflected in alkyl chain length, dipole
moment, positions of substituents, types and even chiral-
ity123−125. The performance of low-dimensional perovskite
thin  films  is  principally  manifested  by  these  various

It  is  worth  mentioning  that  DJ-type  organic  spacer

unique  structures.  Unfortunately,  reports  of  DJ-type
low-dimensional perovskites for memristor applications
are  still  rare  due  to  difficulty  in  obtaining  high  quality
thin films with preferred morphologies and crystallinity.
Nevertheless, we firmly believe that a more comprehen-
sive understanding in the correlation between the chemi-
cal tuning of organic ligands and the device parameters
will greatly boost this area, which should be considered
for future design of spacer cations.
 
Three-terminal transistor architectures
To date, the two-terminal diode structure of perovskite
memristors has been extensively investigated due to their
simple device structure and scalability for practical appli-
cations. Nevertheless, the stochasticity, significant noise,
and  power- and  time-intensive  filament  formation  in-
duced by electrochemical processes inherently cause de-
structive weight updates126. Additionally, the RS mecha-
nism based on ion migration phenomenon shows poor
long-term plasticity in the absence of an external electric
field since mobile ions could diffuse back to their equi-
librium position. More importantly, a large leakage cur-
rent  is  always  observed  in  two-terminal  devices  due  to
the intrinsic electronic conductivity of perovskites. This
significantly  limits  the  number  of  achievable  conduc-
tance states. In contrast, non-destructive operation is al-
lowed  in  three-terminal  transistor  geometry  because  of
the  parallel  learning  and  signal  transmission,  which  is
beneficial for integrating circuits applications.
 
Diverse applications of low-dimensional perovskite
memristors
The  distinct  advantages  of  low-dimensional  perovskite
memristors such as high‐density integration, multi‐stage
storage,  low  power  consumption,  and  high  operational
stability  make  them  ideal  candidates  for  neuromorphic
computing applications, such as artificial synapse. These
constructed  neuromorphic  networks  can  stimulate  hu-
man learning and sensory mechanisms, which hold great
potential  in  artificial  intelligence  systems,  artificial  sen-
sors,  biomedical  imaging,  etc.  Meanwhile,  inspired  by
the  electronic  skins  with  organic  semiconducting  de-
vices, the integration of analog biomimetic systems based
on  perovskite  memristors  could  redefine  the  relation-
ship between the human body and prostheses. By using a
stretchable  logic  array  architecture  that  detects  tactile
and visual sensations, such a flexible system could repair
physical defects or replace defective parts of the human
body, and additionally might allow the expansion of per-
ceptual abilities.
Overall, the challenges and possible future directions
discussed above are manifold. Enriching the family of or-
ganic spacer cations and improving the long-term stabil-
ity are key steps in further developing low-dimensional
perovskite  memristors.  The  excellent  electrical  perfor-
mance of these RS devices allows for the applications in
artificial  synapse,  neuromorphic  computing,  informa-
tion storage and others. We are confident that this excit-
ing research field will grow more rapidly soon, and many
new  opportunities  will  emerge.  We  hope  that  this  Re-
view will provide a general guideline to the community
and inspire new ideas to researchers in the future.
